title: How does EKS consume VPC IP addresses so quickly (the VPC CNI assigns real VPC IPs to pods), what causes IP exhaustion, and how do you fix/avoid it (add subnets / associate a secondary VPC CIDR, review pod density, prefix delegation, consider IPv6, and monitor IP utilization proactively BEFORE production scale)?
shortTitle: Why EKS Consumes VPC IP Addresses So Quickly, and How to Avoid IP Exhaustion

s1_definition.profdef: In Amazon EKS the default Amazon VPC CNI plugin gives every Pod a real, routable IP address from the VPC subnet rather than an overlay address, so each Pod consumes one usable subnet IP just like an EC2 instance does. Because subnets have a finite IP range and the CNI also pre-allocates warm IPs to each node for fast Pod startup, IP addresses are consumed far faster than Pod count alone suggests. IP exhaustion happens when the subnets run out of free addresses, which blocks new Pods from starting. You avoid it by adding subnets or a secondary VPC CIDR, reducing per-node warm-IP over-allocation, enabling prefix delegation to pack more Pods per ENI, considering IPv6, and monitoring IP utilization before you hit production scale.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India every new teller, instead of sharing a single branch phone line, gets their own direct outside phone number from the city's limited pool. That is wonderful for reaching them directly, but the city only has so many numbers, and the phone company even reserves a block of spare numbers per department in advance so new tellers can start instantly. So the pool drains much faster than the headcount suggests, and one day a new teller cannot start because there are no numbers left. The fix is to get more number ranges allocated, reserve fewer spares per department, or move to a vastly larger numbering scheme.
s1_definition.oneliner: EKS gives each Pod a real VPC IP and pre-warms spare IPs per node, so subnets drain fast; avoid exhaustion with more CIDR space, prefix delegation, IPv6, and proactive IP-utilization monitoring.

sections.s2_technical:
The Amazon VPC CNI is what makes EKS networking fast and native: because Pods get real VPC IPs, they are reachable directly, security groups and VPC flow logs work naturally, and there is no overlay encapsulation overhead. The cost of that design is IP consumption. Each worker node attaches elastic network interfaces, and each interface can hold a limited number of secondary IPs depending on the instance type. The CNI assigns Pod IPs from those secondary IPs, so the number of Pods a node can run is bounded by how many IPs its interfaces can hold.

The consumption is faster than it looks for two reasons. First, the CNI maintains a warm pool: to start Pods quickly it pre-allocates spare IPs on each node ahead of demand, so a node running ten Pods may be holding twenty or thirty reserved IPs. Multiply that across many nodes and a large fraction of the subnet is reserved but not actively used. Second, Pod churn from frequent deploys constantly cycles IPs, and IPs are not always released instantly, so transient consumption spikes during rollouts.

IP exhaustion is when the subnets backing the node group run out of free addresses. The symptom is new Pods stuck in ContainerCreating with CNI errors about failing to assign an IP, and nodes that cannot schedule more Pods even though they have spare CPU and memory. This is a capacity-planning failure, not a code bug, and it tends to bite exactly when you scale toward production because that is when Pod and node counts climb.

The fixes form a toolkit. The simplest is to give the VPC more room by adding larger or additional subnets, or associating a secondary CIDR block with the VPC and running node groups there, which immediately enlarges the address pool. I tune the warm-pool behavior with the CNI environment variables that control how many spare IPs each node pre-allocates, trading slightly slower Pod startup for far less reservation waste. The most impactful fix on IPv4 is prefix delegation, where instead of assigning individual secondary IPs the CNI assigns each interface a slash-twenty-eight prefix of sixteen addresses, dramatically increasing how many Pods a node supports and reducing API churn. For a genuinely large platform the strategic answer is IPv6, where the address space is effectively unlimited and exhaustion stops being a concern. The non-negotiable practice is proactive monitoring: I watch subnet free-IP counts and the CNI's available-IP metric and alert well before utilization gets high, because the right time to discover an IP shortage is during capacity planning, not when a production deploy stalls. The senior point is that this is a design consequence of the native-IP model, so it must be planned at VPC design time, not patched under pressure.
sections.s3_banking:
At the National Bank of India our EKS platform grew from a pilot to production, and IP exhaustion nearly caused an outage, which is why this is a real lesson rather than a theoretical one.

Problem 1 — during a scale-up for a festive-season load test, new Transfer Service Pods got stuck in ContainerCreating with CNI "failed to assign IP" errors, even though nodes had plenty of CPU and memory. The small pilot subnet had run out of addresses because the CNI warm pool had reserved most of them. This is exactly subnet exhaustion from native-IP plus warm-pool reservation.

Problem 2 — we needed a durable fix, not just a one-time subnet bump, because growth would continue. This is exactly why we associated a secondary CIDR, enabled prefix delegation to pack far more Pods per node, and added proactive alerting on subnet free IPs.

The mini-project is a runnable Java simulation of a `VpcSubnet` with a finite IP pool, a `VpcCni` that assigns Pod IPs and maintains a warm pool, and an `IpCapacityPlanner` that reports utilization, raises an alert before exhaustion, and shows how prefix delegation and a secondary CIDR expand capacity. We try to schedule Transfer Service Pods serving Rajesh and Priya, hit exhaustion, then apply the fixes and succeed.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile and run the IPAM simulation
javac -d out src/main/java/com/bank/ipam/*.java
java -cp out com.bank.ipam.IpamDemo

# Real EKS: enable prefix delegation + tune warm pool on the VPC CNI
kubectl set env ds aws-node -n kube-system ENABLE_PREFIX_DELEGATION=true
kubectl set env ds aws-node -n kube-system WARM_PREFIX_TARGET=1
# Associate a secondary CIDR (e.g. 100.64.0.0/16) and add subnets for node groups
aws ec2 associate-vpc-cidr-block --vpc-id vpc-abc --cidr-block 100.64.0.0/16
# Monitor free IPs proactively (CloudWatch / CNI metrics) and alert at 80%
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a small pilot subnet with twenty-seven usable IPs and a warm pool of fourteen per node, then a fix with a large secondary CIDR and prefix delegation.

Step 1 — The first node starts with ten Pods. The CNI reserves the ten Pod IPs plus fourteen warm spares, which is twenty-four IPs from the twenty-seven-address subnet. The planner reports utilization near eighty-nine percent and raises the proactive alert.

Step 2 — A second node tries to start with another ten Pods, needing twenty-four more IPs, but only three are free. The subnet is exhausted, so the allocation fails and the new Pods are stuck in ContainerCreating with a CNI "failed to assign IP" error, even though the nodes have spare CPU and memory.

Step 3 — We apply the durable fix by associating a large secondary CIDR with roughly a thousand usable IPs for the node groups, which immediately enlarges the pool.

Step 4 — We enable prefix delegation so the CNI assigns slash-twenty-eight prefixes of sixteen IPs per slot, and we shrink the warm pool to two spares per node, so reservation waste drops sharply.

Step 5 — Three nodes each start with thirty Pods and allocate successfully from the large pool. The planner reports a low utilization well under the alert threshold. A transfer of fifty thousand rupees from Rajesh to Priya runs successfully because the Pods now have IPs, proving the fix scaled the platform safely.

sections.s6_takeaway:
In Amazon EKS the default Amazon VPC CNI gives every Pod a real, routable VPC IP from the subnet rather than an overlay address. That is a great design because Pods are directly reachable, security groups and flow logs work naturally, and there is no encapsulation overhead, but the consequence is that each Pod consumes a usable subnet IP exactly like an EC2 instance does. So IP addresses are a first-class capacity dimension in EKS, not an afterthought.

They drain faster than Pod count suggests for two reasons. First, each node can only hold a limited number of secondary IPs on its network interfaces depending on instance type, which bounds Pod density. Second, the CNI keeps a warm pool, pre-allocating spare IPs on every node so Pods can start quickly, so a node running ten Pods might be reserving twenty or thirty IPs. Across many nodes, a large fraction of the subnet is reserved but not actively in use, and frequent deploys churn IPs on top of that. Exhaustion is when the subnets run out of free addresses, and the symptom is new Pods stuck in ContainerCreating with CNI errors about failing to assign an IP, even on nodes that still have spare CPU and memory.

The fixes form a toolkit I apply in order of impact. I enlarge the address pool by adding subnets or associating a secondary CIDR block with the VPC. I tune the warm-pool settings so each node reserves fewer spare IPs, trading slightly slower Pod startup for far less waste. The biggest IPv4 lever is prefix delegation, where the CNI assigns each interface a slash-twenty-eight prefix of sixteen addresses, which dramatically increases Pods per node. For a genuinely large platform the strategic answer is IPv6, where address space stops being a constraint. And the non-negotiable practice is proactive monitoring of subnet free IPs and the CNI's available-IP metric, with alerts well before utilization gets high.

In my project at the National Bank of India this nearly caused an outage. During a festive-season scale-up, new Transfer Service Pods got stuck in ContainerCreating with IP-assignment errors because our small pilot subnet had run out of addresses, mostly consumed by the warm pool, even though the nodes had plenty of compute. We fixed it durably by associating a large secondary CIDR, enabling prefix delegation to pack far more Pods per node, shrinking the warm pool, and adding an alert at eighty percent subnet utilization. The lesson I always emphasize is that this is a design consequence of the native-IP model, so IP capacity must be planned at VPC-design time and watched proactively, because the worst possible moment to discover an IP shortage is when a production deploy stalls under load.
